utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Mr. Mladic wishes to be excused after the conclusion of the first session this morning so that he can attend to a visit at the UNDU. A written waiver of attendance and consent to proceed without his presence for the remainder of the day has been signed by Mr. Mladic and will be filed shortly, I understand, as soon as the paperwork gets scanned and sent to the Registry for filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, it's hereby put on the record in the presence of Mr. Mladic himself who can hear what you're saying. Of course, it's up to Mr. Mladic whether or not to waive his right to be present, and the Chamber has no problems whatsoever with it. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ivetic, could you please take care that you avoid that the witness goes far beyond what your questions are. I leave it in your hands for the time being. Good morning, Mr. Dosenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dosenovic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that well. I can hardly hear, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the volume be adjusted. Is it now better, Mr. Dosenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you heard what I earlier said, that you are reminded --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you are still bound by your solemn declaration. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start off where we left off yesterday. First can we have again 1D05787 but not broadcast the same, and we'd want to have page 56 in the Serbian, page 37 in the English. And we left off at the paragraph 11.12.1, listing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -- 6 radio relay routes and ending with radio relay route number 644. Before we address that list, I'd like to ask you about the next line, which says: "This shows that 76 channels were to be monitored ..." Could you please clarify for us the total number of channels that should be reflected in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the number of channels is added up, 0431, 4791, and 0431, 4792, that is a total of 70 channels. When this was typed out, instead of a 0, a 6 was typed out. So it should be 70 channels, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now looking at the routes that are reflected here, I take note that the last one is radio relay route number 644, and the footnote directs us to the document that I yesterday indicated was D879. I'd like to now look at D879 with you.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page of the document in both languages, I think we'll see at number 6 the radio relay route 644, and there are an additional two entries, 7 and 8, on this page of the document in the original Serbian and it continues on to the top of the page in the English. What can you tell us about these additional routes - namely, 0654 and 1052 - which are not printed in paragraph 11.12.1 of your expert report with the other routes that are reflected as coming from this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frequencies were added, handwritten: 0654, number 7; and also --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about in relation to your report. Since these entries are not listed in your report, what do you want to tell us about the omission of these entries from your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of channels in this document on the first and second page, that's included in the 70 channels. However, I'm saying that this entire page was omitted during typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So these additional two entries for number 7 and number 8, should we consider them as being part of that paragraph that we just looked at in your report? Is that how I'm to understand what you're saying? And that's paragraph 11.12.1.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could return to 1D05787, and again let's not broadcast it just to be on the safe side. And if we could turn to page 66 in the Serbian and page 44 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see a -- well, we'll wait for the English. Oh, there it is. I see in the original Serbian a quadrant box that says: a, b, c, d. And then it says underneath: "Photograph no. 4 (from the internet)." But we already have a photograph number 4 earlier in your report. What can you tell us about these two items that are on the last page of your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we also see the relevant English?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's on the bottom of the page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the box is not there, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what can you tell us about these two items that I've drawn our attention to on this last page?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During scanning, it got to this page out of carelessness. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do we need to consider these two items as part of your report or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, apart from these corrections that we've gone through today and yesterday, do you believe the remainder of your report to be correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by your report from the perspective of your knowledge, experience, and expertise in military communications?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for the report to be marked for identification, to be tendered later on after completion of all questioning and submissions by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait for that moment. Nevertheless, Mr. Ivetic, I'm still puzzled by the line: "When the number of channels is added up," and then a few numbers appear, "that is a total of 70 channels." I have got no idea what is added up there. Certainly not the numbers there. I'm just lost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- spell that out for us with the witness in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could then return to page 37 in the English and page 56 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looked as if these were ERN numbers in the footnote 48, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that relates to document D879 that we looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what actually is added is the number of routes that is found on those pages? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The number of channels in those routes that are found on those pages, as each route --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- has multiple channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now I better understand what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if I may add to the confusion. That sentence that Judge Orie referred to gives the total of 70 with respect to route 644 only. What about the other five routes that are mentioned on that list?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says "not including," so that -- that 70 channels is everything except for route 0674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the correction is, first of all, to the reference to 76, which should be "70," and the text reads: "This shows that now 70 channels were to be monitored not including the secure channels on radio relay route number 0674."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness now refers to ERN numbers of -- well, of -- looked at military [indiscernible] which are not in evidence yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are. It's D879. It's an exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have missed that. Apologies for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the document is to be marked for identification awaiting further submissions and a decision on admission. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D1187 MFI. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1187 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need to have it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we do. There are some parts that should be under seal, so we should do the whole thing under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like to follow up with some items from your report that has now been marked D1187, MFI, under seal. Let's look first at page 3 in both languages and paragraph number 2 of the same. And in the middle of that paragraph, you say: "The ABH had RP-2M, 2-12MHz frequency banned interception devices of domestic (Yugoslav) manufacture ..." What kind of devices or transmissions did these have the ability to intercept?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to establishment, all brigades of the Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia had this RP-2M with 2 to 12 megahertz frequency band, and it was supposed to report on enemy flights. So I'm certain that the brigades in the Army of BH, as in the Army of Republika Srpska, had these receivers, and with them one could follow radio traffic from 2 to 12 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the continuation of this paragraph, you identify reception devices of the Japanese firm Ikon, Kenwood, and the AOR, which were the basis of the ABH interception system. Were these devices what would be considered professional military grade or amateur grade manufactured devices?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mentioned pieces of equipment, Japanese made, could have been obtained in the free market, and they were only for ham radio operators and other structures. People who dealt with communications by way of a hobby. And then also there were some companies that used this. The only piece of equipment here that had a military version was, I mean, 450S. It had a military version. The rest, no. And, of course, such devices are weaker than professional devices that armies had and still have. Units equipped for electronic surveillance, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you to explain the last part of your answer that you gave when you said: "Such devices are weaker than professional devices"? What does that mean in terms of the technical capabilities or operation of those devices?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it means: When a device is manufactured, everyone who places an order says what the technical capacity should be. So the devices of the Army of BiH were such that they probably wanted to hear the participants that were far away. However, when the army asks for that, they want to hear a participant that they are following even outside the range. So that's the essence. So these receivers are a lot more sensitive and they can operate in all weather and other conditions, whereas the former are not equipped in that way. That is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you could clarify once again. You said: "These receivers are a lot more sensitive and they can operate in all weather and other conditions, whereas the former are not equipped that way." Could you tell us which receivers are more sensitive? Was it the amateur grade or the professional military grade that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The devices that the BH Army had, Japanese made, these are devices that are intended for civilian structures, and they do not have the kind of performances that professional ones do, those that are ordered by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, of the two types - the types ordered by the military or the amateur ones for civilians - which are more sensitive? Which receivers are more sensitive?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military devices are always more sensitive. And as I have said, they need to meet other challenges, like the configuration of the land, weather, and the way in which they are being used. It's not the same as if you use something in a tent, a dugout, et cetera, or something that you use in an office where the temperature is always right and so on and so forth, when there is no dust, when there are no other influences of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now looking at paragraph 3 on the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on. Witness, you have told us what type of equipment the BH had and sensitivity, civilian use, military use. What's the basis of your knowledge for what exactly was within the BiH available as equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know what the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had on the basis of the documents that were provided to me by the law office. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the basis for it is the documentation you received from the Defence, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us then exactly what you received? Do you have a list or what is it that you received from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Defence I received a document, I mean, about the devices that stations north and south had; those interception stations. And then on the internet, I found these pieces of equipment, I photographed them -- or rather, scanned them and attached them to my paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you are saying that your answers are based on information the Defence provided to you and on what you found on the internet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we'll get to it later, Your Honours, but I can already let the parties know 1D01081 and 1D01082 are, I believe, the documents for the northern and southern facilities that the witness has just mentioned. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber then, of course, expects to -- in the best way possible that it's already clear from the report what the sources of information are. But at least it's good to hear that we'll hear more about it soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 3 on the same page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you say in talking about the level of measures implemented by the 2nd Corps, and procedures were similar in other corps, made for minimum chance of interception. Can you tell us: Were these measures that were being undertaken by the 2nd Corps undertaken to any specific orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All measures that were taken with a view to protecting the communications system are studied during schooling. That's the way it was in the JNA. That is prescribed by rules, how one should act in a particular way. It wasn't that any special order was written up during the war, because that went without saying that this had to be done. However, if there were to be some violation - and this kind of thing did happen - and if there were some shortcomings in terms of electronic surveillance, then that would happen. The 2nd Corps did the same thing too, because the communications people in all the units were trained in the same schools. So it is only natural that they took the same measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at page 5 in both languages and -- I'll wait for that. Looking at item or paragraph number 1.1.4, here you mention the PTT service and its use. How was the PTT service used by communication units of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications system of the Army of Republika Srpska was linked into the other communications systems, mostly with the PTT. When it was necessary, certain devices and lines were appropriated for the use of the Army of Republika Srpska, and this link can best be seen in this diagram here in Attachment 6 where you can see that we used underground cables of the PTT, also the wire overland connections, and then also some services from the PTT to transfer military communications. The cooperation went so far that perhaps if some post office was within the zone, then they would work together with the army communications units but they wouldn't leave their places of work. They would just be carrying out instructions given by some organ of the corps or any other unit that happened to be in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about these PTT systems when used in this manner by the army? What can you tell us about any civilian or consumer use of those systems during that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we just clear up which army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in the context you referred to the VRS, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have difficulties in looking at it in any other way. When Mr. Ivetic referred to "the army," it's the VRS, Witness. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what can you tell us about these PTT systems when used in a manner that you described by the VRS in terms of civilian or consumer use of those same systems during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using the PTT communications occurred if it was in a combat zone, then the civilian sector didn't have any need to use that service. But mostly the PTT exchanges were located in the depth, while air or underground cables were also in combat zones and they frequently linked the PTT centres of the entire former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, for example, if we take Kupres and Bugojno, there would be a line. That line remained in place, and our side used it for military tasks from Kupres to the line of separation. And then if the B and H Army was there, it would be from the line of separation with the Army of Republika Srpska to Bugojno. So then it was all covered. While, for example, post offices in all places also provided services to the civilian structures; thus, taking certain capacities and resources was not supposed to interfere with the actual work of all the PTT facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would there be military and civilian traffic on the same PTT network simultaneously and the same resources within the PTT network?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible. For example, if it was a permanent connection, one line would be taken by the army. And then if there were two, three, four, the rest would be used by the PTT. They could loan the use of one line. And if it was essential, an order would be issued so that a certain amount of the resources or the capacity would be loaned to the army for their needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to that in this example you said "one line that could be taken by the army," would there be civilian traffic on that one line taken by the army?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it. If it was that kind of route, the civilian sector would not be using it because they would not be covering the area that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska at the other end. So, for example, the PTT had no need for such a route, and then the army would be using it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to page 8 in English and page 10 in the Serbian and look at 3.4.7. And I believe we need to go to page 10 in the Serbian -- or 8 -- no, 10, 10. 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph, 3.4.7, you are talking about communications systems of the MUP and municipalities. Did the VRS utilise or enter into these communication networks of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said here, there were others who had communication systems, such as the Ministry of the Interior, the centres for alerting, then also the electric utilities system, radio, television, and so on. The army did not use those systems and did not take any of those devices. It just acted in cooperation with these people. Perhaps they used or exchanged telephone lines; for example, if the Ministry of the Interior was engaged on a task, they had their own communications system and we did not use that system, but we did have a device to communicate with the commanding officer from that task and from that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've answered my next question, so now we can move to page 9 in the English and page 11 in the Serbian. And paragraph 4.5. And here you talk about both MUP and PTT equipment at features in addition to army equipment at communications features. Can you tell us who maintained each type of equipment? That is to say, army equipment, MUP equipment, PTT equipment.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications conducted through radio relay nodes were located at certain salient features and elevations in order to be able to maintain the communications properly. At these features, we often had devices from the army, the Ministry of the Interior, and the PTT, and everybody would have their own rooms and their own devices at that facility. They had common logistics, if I may use a military term for that, and combat support. But everything else -- and also at a higher level, the use of frequencies was coordinated as well as the system of cooperation among these different users.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do we now know who maintained that equipment? Because that was the question. You told about coordination, you told about use, but who maintained that equipment? Apparently that's what you want to know, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each of the users maintained their own equipment. Assistance -- mutual assistance was never ruled out, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 10 in the English and page 12 in the Serbian of your report, and you have there diagram number 2. And I believe if we look at 1D05788, we should have a bigger, clearer photograph of that diagram.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now we have it in both languages. Now, could you briefly explain for us what the colours and the denotations on the original mean in terms of what is depicted?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications in the Army of Republika Srpska ended at the command post, while the final users were the commanders at the operations centres and also at the telephone exchange. What we see here is a diagram that was used by the personnel working in the operations centre. And they were supposed to know how to set up communications with specific units; which means if it was a wire link, then the system of securing the link was lower. But if it was a radio relay communications, then they had to stick to strict rules for encryption of data. For example, here in red we see in the middle it says "11 lpbr." Communications with that unit were maintained only via radio relay links. I'm sorry. So the colour red leading to the 11th Light Infantry Brigade indicates a radio relay link which means that they needed to pay attention to data protection. And then this was also linked with their operations centre, because operations centres were also linked amongst themselves from the Main Staff towards the corps and the other commands. Then you had the direct phone line of the commander, that was linked in as well as all the others. Could I please look at the right side of the diagram? This is going to the left. I need the other side, please. All right. This is good. At the bottom underneath, we have these rectangles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't touch the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And they are part of a large rectangle representing units. So if a communication -- if a communication line -- actually, if the rectangular has nothing on it, that means that that link is maintained by an induction telephone. For example, with the 5th Light Infantry Brigade, the 3rd Light Infantry Brigade as well, if there is -- if the rectangle is crossed with one line, one diagonal line such as the 9th Light Infantry Brigade, then that indicates that the communication is maintained through a telephone exchange. It's not directly linked. If there are two lines in the rectangle, that means that the communications are maintained directly through the PTT by dialling an automatic telephone number which is connected to that exchange. And so you have these -- motorised battalion and another battalion. That's the case with them. And both of those units were in Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could tender 1D05788 as the next public exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the problem is in the English translation. The legend is missing, at least on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see if it's on page 2. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the connecting lines between the boxes are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know. Yeah, the legend is on this page. And, unfortunately, this is how we received it from CLSS, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you receive something which is incomprehensible for the Judges, you say it comes from CLSS so therefore we present it to the Judges. Is that the position the Defence takes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's why I have it side by side with the original, and I've asked him to explain the coloured lines on the original. That's, I believe, been the practice in this case when there's documents, when there is diagrams that are not shown that there are translations of the notations, and the diagram one looks at the original. That's the way we've been doing it since the beginning. That's why I put them side by side so Your Honours could see the colours and the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood the previous conversation. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you could just repeat the 1D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it's 1D05788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then could we hear from the witness, from the legend on the second page in the English, the dotted line, the third in the legend, could you tell us what that stands for? Can you read it? You see that, Witness? No, I'd like to have it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how it was translated. The dotted line indicates an induction line. It's a communication maintained by an induction telephone. A field telephone. One that you use by turning the handle on it. So it's a field telephone. And you can use it in the same way that you use a normal telephone, but it's just not a direct line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what does it read? How does it read, literally? So the first line is RR, the second line is wire link --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Induction direct line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. McCloskey? Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D1188. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to your report, which is D1187, marked for identification, under seal, and turn to page 13 in the Serbian and page 10 in the English. We have here a diagram at number 3 as an example of the working of the telephone centrals at the 2nd Krajina Corps, Obrazac DV1. For this, I'd like to call up 1D5789, which should be the original and translation. And we see here also that there are colours in relation to the lines on the original Serbian document. Could you please confirm for us if those colours are -- mean the same as they do in the one we just looked at or if it's something different?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again here, the coloured lines indicate different ways that telephone exchanges are connected. So the red colour indicates that the communication is maintained through a radio relay link.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where would these forms be posted or made available in a corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This diagram would be part of the documents of the commander of the communications battalion that is facilitating the connections. They would come to me as the chief, and they would be issued to other commanding officers who were actually executing these communications so that they know how the communications were organised, with which units, and on how many channels, and this would be along the line of the exchanges, the operation centres, and the commander. This diagram would not be sent to other commanding officers or senior officers in the corps, only to a communications unit's senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see in the middle for the 2nd KKKM, which I believe is "command centre," "command post," we see the term "oblak." What is "oblak"?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This form is given in the rules for communications. This is form DV1. According to that form, the telephone exchanges are represented by a circle. The central circle is the main exchange for that unit. And it's divided into three parts: The top part is where the name of the unit is, by establishment; for example, the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Then underneath that, there is the secret name, that's "oblak," and then that same thing applies to the other smaller exchanges. The links connecting them - for example, the first line on the left, it's quite small, but it says "album," that's the secret name - and then there is a small circle split into two where in the upper half of the circle there is the number of the telephone channels and at the bottom there is the number of the telegraph channels, the teleprinter links. Some units that had teleprinters could also maintain teleprinter communications. But those who were not supposed to have it by establishment, did not have teleprinter links. So then the diagram would indicate to the officer what kind of communications he could have with the other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D5789 at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D1189. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Any need to have it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we return to your report, which is D1187, marked for identification, under seal, and look at page 17 in the Serbian and page 12 in the English. And -- I'll wait for the English. Here in paragraph 5.3, you are talking about Jastrebac documents. Now, I want to know a little bit more about these documents. To understand when you say: "They could be used without fear of disclosure even though all the armies after 1991 had them," could you please explain to us how that can be.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jastrebac documents were drafted by the JNA. There were nine books in that set of documents; secret names, call signs, ID tables, frequencies of all the devices, and I mean radio relay devices as well. And so this was drafted army by army and from republic to republic for each one. When the former JNA disintegrated, all the newly formed armies, up until a certain time, kept those documents and operated according to the documents. There was no fear that data could be leaked unless there was interception. Those who did the interception knew that these documents were being used. They knew the other armies, the manner in which they operated, their documents, and so on. So here we have the ID table. That book has 99 pages. And the chief of communications, when he tells his subordinates which table to use, he would say, let's say, table 7555, and then he would provide the key for the use of that particular table, because without a key it wouldn't mean anything. So he would provide the key, and now those who wanted to identify their collocutors, they would, for example, ask, and I'm going to give you an example: They would say "86," and then when you look at the intersection between those two numbers, you see the number 988, which means that that is correct. And then that number is immediately crossed off, and it cannot be used anymore for as long as this table is in use. And then for each subsequent operation, a new document would be issued and that, of course, implies new tables. And that would be a new table for the call signs, for frequencies, for secret names, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can break at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take break and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. The Chamber is considering to adapt the schedule but is still busy making the necessary calculations where, as is now also put on the record, Mr. Mladic has waived his right to be present and is not in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, meanwhile you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at paragraph 5.4 of your report, and it's the last line in B/C/S before going on to the next page in Serbian, and it is the last sentence in English, it says that the A-B key was difficult to decode because numbers were changed by machine or out of a hat. Could you please explain how that would work? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Keys are the basis for the protection of this table, so it's not the table itself. It's the keys. The keys were made by machine, and this was done by the communications organ. In a situation when there wouldn't be the right kind of equipment to make a key, and then on little pieces of paper numbers would be made, written down from 01 to 99 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then all these little pieces of paper would be put into a hat and then numbers would be taken out - 10, 20, 30, no matter how many are needed. And I've already said that once a certain number is used from the list, then that one is crossed out and it cannot be given again. And for each and every operation and for a certain number of days, there is always a different table and, of course, a different key.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back one page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When referring to a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can zoom in on the photograph at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When referring to a key, which part of the table represents the keys that would be done by machine or out of a hat?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner in this table it says B-A; that is to say, column B is the horizontal key and column A is the vertical. So what I said: One number from the horizontal, one from the vertical, and then the number that is the ID is obtained in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is an original with an English translation, it's 1D5791 of this table, but I will not be tendering it as I don't think it adds much to the comprehensions and [indiscernible] numbers involved and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's pretty clear as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we can look page 17 in the Serbian and page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You identify in footnote number 18, talking of instructions for identifications in telephone and radio communications from the internet which show that the Croats used that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just briefly look at 1D5792.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could it be a different number? This one isn't in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D05792 is what I have listed. I think I'll just move on and we'll come back to that if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at, staying in your report, then, page 24 in the Serbian and page 18 in the English. And here you are describing diagram 4 in the English, whereas it's the page where the diagram is in the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could see 1D05796 in e-court. And if we wait for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is this the same schematic that we just looked at in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same. Except that this one is a lot clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look for a moment. The name of the unit that is just below Dubrava, could you please read that into the record as the translation does not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rectangle here, Dubrava, between the triangle and the circle, what is written, it is the 3rd lpbr ; that is to say, the 3rd Light Infantry Brigade, and there is radio communication with it. Up there in that rectangle, you can see a triangle where says "inside 20," and above it it says "30," which means that it is radio network 30, and "VF" is used. Also, "VVF," these circles, next to the circle it says 31 and also it says 2/2 in the circle, and that means "VVF/22K" that has a protection device on it. In addition to that, to the far right, there is another circle where it says 12. That is a reserve radio network in case another unit gets involved if there is a combat operation going on and so on, or if it is necessary to organise an entire network. Documents are planned, reserve documents for these reserve devices, or rather reserve radio networks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek -- You said in the triangle we see "20" and then above it it says "30." Is that in the Dubrava --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that in the Dubrava box or is it in the Livada box which is just above the Dubrava box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says "Dubrava," I've explained that that is the 3rd Light Infantry Brigade, and it communicates with the superior command up there where it says Livada. And then in that triangle, it says which radio networks are involved and which units are subordinated to this Livada, if we should call it that. That's the command, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I now better understand what you meant. I also noticed that apparently some changes or redactions have been made in the Dubrava box. It looks as if pencil writing has been rubbed out and replaced. Do you know anything about that? Do you know why there were changes and when they were made and whether they were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document, as can be seen in the upper right-hand corner, was elaborated for an operation called Grmec. So this is a working document. I attached it. These are my documents that I worked on, and probably during the course of this work something had to be changed, improved, something had to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it dates from what time, Operation Grmec was when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, as far as I can remember it was in 1994. Sometime at Suva Medja. That's Bosnia-Herzegovina, across the Una, on the left bank. I'm not 100 per cent sure but I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's just used as an example as to how it works for operations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the names we have along the right-hand side - Livada, Dubrava, then one that cannot be read, Grude, Bastilja, Djoker and another one that cannot be read - what are those -- what are those names?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the rectangle, it says that the unit has an establishment name. Grude, for example, is the 15th Brigade. So on the right-hand side, you actually have the secret names, the code names of these units. And it's only the organiser of the communication that uses this document. It's not the operators. It's stations that use this document. They don't know which unit is involved. They just know the code names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But can you identify the word between Dubrava and Grude? Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it says "Oroz."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And perhaps we can scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oroz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And then we see Djoker. And below that, what could that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Underneath Djoker?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's written like "this." It seems to be the word "this." Now why, I mean, you know, it's a working document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were documents that were my personal documents, and I always carried them with me, and that is how these documents reached you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now then tender this document, which is 1D05796.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D1190. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1190 is admitted into evidence. Now, all the other names are translated for us, such as Dubrava being "forest." What does "Oroz" mean? And I don't expect you to explain that in English, but perhaps where the transcript says "Oroz," whether that is an existing word and what it means, this is a question to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I the one who is supposed to give an answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you are not supposed -- well, unless you would know what the word "Oroz" means in English, then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I know what Oroz means. In Serbian, Oroz means -- well, there is two things. For example, on an old-fashioned rifle, the part that is cocked in order to hit the cap, that is called Oroz, that is one meaning. And Oroz is also a chicken; or to be more precise, a rooster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, now we have a broad choice of how to understand it next to the forest, the snowball, the Bastilja and the Djoker. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could return to D1187, marked for identification, under seal, and if we could turn to page 21 in the English and page 28 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking at paragraph 8.2.5 on this page, you say here that the VRS used existing nodes and set up RR CV at Mount Ozren, Veliki Zep, and Gucevo. Does that mean that these nodes did not previously exist prior to the formation of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that these were newly established ones, that is to say, up until the war, they did not exist. The Main Staff came to Crna Rijeka, to that area, and then there was this former JNA facility there, and then Veliki Zep was built there, the radio relay node. Then down there, above Mostar - Velez, that's it - there was also a radio relay node. It was taken by the HVO, however. So for the Herzegovina Corps, a new radio relay node was built at Leotar. Because of communications with VRS units on the left bank of the Drina river, it was a problem to establish communications, so the conclusion was reached that a new node should be placed on the right bank of the Drina river. And then with the agreement of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia government, the VRS was allowed to use its own resources to build a new node at Mount Gucevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, just for purposes of clarifying the record, could you please repeat the name of that last mountain that was built with the permission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia government.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the mountain is Gucevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now turn to page 23 in English of your report, and it will be pages 32 through 33 in the Serbian. We have another diagram, and I'd like to look at 65 ter number 1D05800. And now in your report at paragraph 8.2.16, you say: "The marked participants, marked yellow in the diagram, are linked by radio relay communications. Use of general KZ documents required." Now, while we are here looking at the document, we can see which ones are marked in yellow. Can you tell us what are KZ documents or KZ documents?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This diagram shows the plan of communications for carrying out an operation for the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps. And then further down, the operations centre, OC, was established for carrying out that operation. IFP 11 is an intercom that links ten participants. Five of them use radio relay communications. Since there wasn't equipment for cryptographic encoding, then general documents by way of a crypto-encryption had to be used. Beforehand, it was called TKT, "secret command over troops." That includes a map, other equipment, a signals table, and other documents that were needed and, of course, a key, so that the coded map and coded tables could be used. That is the general way in which this encryption functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how would the use of KZ documents affect what would be talked about over open transmissions -- over open -- or "unsecured," I guess, is the better word, transmissions.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an encoder is attached to the basic equipment, whoever were to hear it would hear some tones, some sounds that would be totally unintelligible. This person could not understand any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could clarify. I think what I said -- the acronym I used has been misrelayed to you. Let me use the old acronym: How would the use of TKT documents affect what was talked about in open transmissions?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General documents for encoding are used for transferring certain orders, tasks, so that it would not be open, unsecured. Otherwise, if the enemy was listening in, then they would see clearly what our intentions were. However, with the TKT it can be heard, but again it's some kind of numbers and some words that would not actually provide any kind of information to whoever may be listening in. This person would not know what this is all about. Of course, whoever is an experienced interceptor will realise that these are coded documents. However, quite a bit of time would be needed to decode that communication, and time is important so perhaps it would be too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go back in the English one page. I see what looks like a footnote or not with some 15, 16 items, the first one RRV; the second, IKM -- oh, I now see. That relates to the entries throughout this document and it's not corresponding with the -- what follows under 51721, and that is found on the second page. I now understand what it is, but it took me a while. I'm always a bit slow. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit 1191. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could now go back to your expert report, D1187, marked for identification, under seal. And if we could look at page 26 in the English and page 37 in the Serbian. In 8.4 - that is, 8.4.1 and 8.4.2 - you talk about courier communications, and you say that the courier did not have the key. Was this method of delivery used for anything other than just confidential documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's based upon what's in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, the question. Is the question not a leading question? Shouldn't the question be: What was it used for?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except that that's in 8.4.2, Your Honours. Couriers carrying documents, i.e., mail, had combat support required that the bag carried the courier would be locked. The courier carrying the mail did not have the key." So my question is: Apart from the confidential documents and mail, was this system used for anything else. This method, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't used for other purposes. Only for confidential mail; that is to say, orders, reports, and so on. Then the operations organ of the superior command would most often pack this in a bag, lock it, and give it to a courier. The courier would take a vehicle and armed escort they would reach the operations organ of the unit that it was sent to. The operations organ does have the key of that bag. Then it's unlocked, and then the procedure is carried out properly. All the signatures are there, et cetera, and then it is returned. And then that is how these documents for encoding were transported, in this locked bag. For some ordinary mail, something that is not confidential or personal mail during the war, that was not used. It was just done regularly as one does nowadays in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have said that this is how documents for encoding were transported. Could you please specify which documents for encoding you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant there are tapes with keys and the code used to encrypt the speech when you are making an encrypted telegram at the cryptographic data protection centre. These are just perforated ribbon. And there are also tables for encryption that are packed in non-see through - so opaque and waterproof - packaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now at 9.3 on the same page in English but on the next page in the Serbian, among the protection measures used, you say was the use of stick antennas was forbidden for devices having directional antennas. Could you explain for us the difference between these two type of antennas, a stick antenna and a directional antenna?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain devices, such as RRU-1, have stick antennas. And if we look and think that it looks like this pencil, it broadcasts on all sides radially. And the other antenna is placed horizontally, and it broadcasts in certain directions, and so the broadcasting to the side is reduced to a minimum and it will broadcast toward the front. The construction can vary, it's not exactly like a pencil, but that would be the direction in which they are broadcasting. So that would be the difference between a stick and a directional antenna. There are, of course, other types with different types of emission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Between a stick and a directional antenna, which is more suited to transmit over greater distances and why?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directional antennas are better for longer distances. They have a greater range, if I can put it that way, because the power is directed in one direction, and that's why the signal is stronger than if you were to measure it around the stick antenna. That's why they're better. However, stick antennas have a slightly different purpose and reasons why, in some situations, they are better.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which type of antenna would be used for a radio relay device such as an RRU-800 or FM200 as opposed to radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: RRU-800 uses helio antennas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if that is the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and they are placed on a pole that is 7 metres high. There is an emission and -- a transmission and a receiver antenna. It's a little bit different, but it's also a type of a directional antenna. And it's radial. There are a number of elements that make up that antenna, but it's also directional and it's placed on a pole. And then it depends on the purpose, what the height of the pole would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, isn't it true that we spent already hours on radio relay, how it was directed, what problems it caused for intercepting it, et cetera, et cetera? Now, for me it's new that it's on a pole, but if that's what you wanted to establish ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I was trying with our very first expert on this matter to talk about the difference between stick and directional antennas. Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we've heard that, and then you've continued to ask what type of antenna was used for radio relay device, and we've heard that from all those in the field several times. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can then turn to page 28 of your report in English and page 39 in Serbian. And here in your report we have diagram number 10, which is described on the next page in Serbian, but I'd like to look at 1D5803 with you, which should be the same diagram just, of course, with translation and perhaps a little bit clearer than we see here.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the diagram of secure communications of the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps with the Main Staff, radio relay devices FM200, with a device --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the acronyms of the devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat the acronyms of the devices, but I suggest we also break it down so it's easier to know what you are talking about for those that are working off the English which does not, at this moment, have the part that's to the left of the chart. Sir, if I can ask you: First of all, we see on the left there is a triangle with the number 200 noted in it. What does this particular part of the diagram depict?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's start from the left and then move to the right. In the instructions of communications documents, there is a rule as to how equipment should be drawn. So the triangle with the straight line and then another line under a 45-degree angle and a little line indicates device, radio relay device 200. So it's not a 9. It's 2-0-0. Perhaps somewhere there is the number 9. It's the same device, RRU-9, which is manufactured in Yugoslavia. It's the same as the FM200. That is connected to the encryption device, KZU-71. Then that is connected to the carrying frequency device AMD-310, and then those devices have eight channels. And we have here which channel goes to whom; for example, number 1, commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps; then commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska; and then you have the operations centre, communications; then you have communications with the neighbouring units - the Krajina Corps, the 15th Corps of the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina; then there is the protected telephone from the automatic telephone exchange in Banja Luka - this is the stationary centre in Banja Luka, which means that's the military exchange. One channel was defective and one was free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could we seek -- you said that the same as the FM200 was connected to the encryption device KZU-71. Do we see that anywhere in here, or is it just that you explained to us that that's how it was done? Could you tell us whether it's found somewhere in this diagram or whether it's just that you are explaining that this is, although it doesn't appear here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the encryption device is not in the diagram, but it was used in the actual operation. You can also see it from the heading, that it's a secure communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Now, I think that in the English version that the text written vertically is AMD-340. You said, however, it's AMD-310. Could I just be sure that it is AMD-310 or is it AMD-340?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you zoom in, you can see that it's a 1 and that the correct acronym would be AMD-310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This may be a misinterpretation in the transcription of the original into the English version. I think it's not of such essence that we would need to find a new one, but it's at least on the record now that it should be read "AMD-310." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, could these secure channels transmitting over the FM200 via the AMD-310, could they be both listened to and understood as recognisable speech by someone who was not an intended participant in the transmission?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could listen into the channels if you were along that route and if you had a device of the same characteristics on the same frequency, same modulation, and so on and so forth. But if the line was secure, they would not understand anything that they heard. I already said this before, they could just hear some crackling or some tones, but there would be nothing intelligible. They could record it and then try to de-scramble it by using different devices. Perhaps somebody would have devices which could decode the signal. But the B and H Army did not have such devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the source of your knowledge, that they didn't have them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that by using a document which I received after I wrote my document here, and it's a report by one of the commanders of either the north or south location, to his superior, where they say, for example: You are asking for our position, please don't ask that anymore because we don't have anything in order to be able to find out which location it is and the Chetniks don't want to tell us, either. So it's much simpler to have locators than to have decoding devices. That's my conclusion. Had they been able to decode the interception, then they would have been able to work out the positions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you know the location, you have not yet decoded it in any way. But let me just try to understand your last answer. It's translated as: "Had they been able to decode the interception," that is, to decode the intercepted signals. And you say: "... then they would have been able to work out the positions as well." Could you explain how they could have done that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In orders, or in conversations conducted through secure links, frequently they would mention -- it was open communication when it was written, but in speech it was secure. But then frequently you would mention command posts, commanding officers, locations of stations, and so then they wouldn't have had to look for positions in 1995 of the Army of Republika Srpska. This is what I was referring to from the time of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you're saying if the content of the conversations would give a clue to locations, then it would have been easier to find out in that way rather than by other means to establish the location of the various units. Is that -- or command posts or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One other question in relation to this, that is: The diagram is about secure communications, secure channels. You earlier told us that the encryption device is not here. Was there any way to use those channels without using the encryption device so as to bypass it or to switch it off or whatever? So could you use these channels if you wished to without secure the signals through the encryption devices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A radio relay communication, the FM200, can work normally with the carrying frequency device without the encryption device, and then the communication is not coded. The diagram shown here was my working document, and simply during that time you often didn't have enough time to do more, and so then I omitted to indicate that the data encryption device was used here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but also could not be used, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all the diagrams and communications, you can see that there were many devices that did not have a data encryption device. But then, you would use different types of protection. For example, in RRU-800 you cannot protect the whole group. Only specific channels. Then the other channels would transmit speech, as such. But then the communication would be protected by general encryption data protection documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But if you would be negligent, could you send signals and forget or negligently do not encrypt or otherwise protect the communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in these documents, there is a diagram of protected radio relay communications of the Army of Republika Srpska where the Main Staff of the VRS has secure connections, one group of such connections with each of the corps. So there could be no talk of negligence. You have the original diagram with all the devices included. This would be given to the commander of the unit who actually executed those communications, so he could not do anything that was not negligent. And if I was having any question about it, I would ask if the data encryption device was being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say there could be no talk of negligence, is that because technically it was impossible, or whether it was clearly against instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, it's technically impossible. If I am negligent on one end, the person at the other end is not. So then if the commander of the Main Staff would call the commander of the 2nd Corps and the encryption device is not switched on at his end, he will not hear him at all. In order for them to hear each other, the equipment has to be identical at both ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's impossible to at both ends just ignore or switch off, or whatever you would call it, the encryption devices; both in sending and receiving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that would constitute sabotage at the very least. If an order was issued that you must establish a connection with encryption data protection, then that would be sabotage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Technically possible but sabotage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that would not be negligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To add on to what you just discussed, could you explain for us -- now, you told us the diagram where the KZ-71 encryption device would be located, so let's talk in terms of actuality. The radio relay nodes that are usually up on mountains and then the command centres are usually somewhere on lower ground. Where in that schematic or system would the KZU-71 be attached?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KZU-71 device would be attached at the end of the radio relay station. As I said, you would have the IMD frequency carrier, then you would have the telephone line to the end user, the commander, the operations centre and so on and so forth. And then this RRU-800 would go to the radio relay node. And then through greater multiplexes, such as V4 or the SMC radio relay devices, it would go to the end node and it would split off from there to be received by another RRU-800, and then you would have the same sequence of devices connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I guess --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think we've tendered this yet. I can either tender it or mark it for identification if we need to revisit the translation of AMD-340. I leave that in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we established that -- it's having been put on the record that AMD-340 should be read in the English version as "AMD-310" and that for the time being would be sufficient. Therefore, you tender it? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D1192. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber made its calculations. We'll continue now until 12.30, then we'll take a break of half an hour. And from 1.00 we'll continue until quarter past 2.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to your report, again D1187, marked for identification, under seal, and if we can look at page 28 in the English, page 41 in the Serbian. Or, actually, before we do that, if we could look at 65 ter number 19848. You mentioned in the prior exchange in answering Judge Orie's questions, a diagram of the secured channels of the GS -- of the Main Staff, and at page 40 of the Serbian, you have -- diagram number 11 of your report, which is identified as document 04336629. Is this that diagram you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could zoom out a little bit on the Serbian or -- I don't know how else to -- maybe can it be flipped. There we go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it. That is the diagram of secure communications between the Main Staff and the corps commands. And then there is the 2nd Krajina Corps in the corner, and this arrived along this radio relay route from the radio relay node Klekovaca through FM200. 0272 is the radio relay route, I think. But it doesn't matter. You can see it. From Klekovaca to Ostrelj where the command post of the 2nd Krajina Corps was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, then I would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D1193. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, we were on page 28 of the English. Could we have that? That's the report of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Footnote 37 refers to analysis of combat readiness, page 37. Do you have any idea where we could find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. One moment. That's a document that we already have in evidence, and I will give you the number in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you find it later, that's okay as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I might have it on my old sheet. It's the -- what it is, it's the analysis of the VRS dating from 1994 as to the work -- 1993 dating to the work from 1992, which we've used with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- if -- most important for us is that we can find the reference and see to what it's related, so if you later could give the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can give you -- we have, I believe, two copies of it in e-court. One copy is 1D05793. And I believe that that is already in evidence as, I think, a P number, but I don't have that at present. I can get back to you with that perhaps after the coming break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm not insisting on receiving it immediately. Although Mr. McCloskey might help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Ivetic is correct. That came in as P00338 and has been discussed by many, many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we have seen quite a lot of documents about combat readiness. And without a year and without further explanations, it would be quite an effort to know exactly what this refers to. But now we do. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at 10.1, which we now have on the screen in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here in your report, you say when the war started there were no EiPED units on the territory of BH. Can you explain what you mean here?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activity. In the territory of Yugoslavia, there were several units for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activity. I am going to mention only some of these locations; for example, near airport Pleso in Zagreb, there is one battalion for that; then in Divulje near Split another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you didn't ask for the locations of such units. Are you interested to know? And what is the use for the Chamber to know exactly where they were located?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I also verify that the translation "reconnaissance surveillance" is not exactly the same, perhaps? I do not know whether that causes any inconvenience and whether you could agree with Mr. McCloskey on what the meaning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He's nodding so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, and if you need the locations, ask for them. Otherwise, proceed otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, under the JNA system, what specific course work or training was required for someone to be qualified as an operator within an EiPED unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training personnel for carrying tasks out in that area was carried out in the School for Electronic Surveillance and Anti-Electronic Activity in Belgrade within the School Centre for Communications, and that is where both NCOs and commissioned officers were trained; that is to say, everyone at their own level. In addition to that, the JNA sometimes had soldiers through contracts for radio reconnaissance. I don't know about other duties, but I know that for that particular field there would be contractors of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long would the training or schooling for EiPED, and especially radio reconnaissance, last?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training went on for a year for officers after they complete the general military academy in Belgrade. Then an additional year at the school centre. Afterwards, some of that was changed when all these changes took place, and then they were trained together with technical personnel in the military institute in Zarkovo, near Belgrade. NCOs were also trained. After basic training in Sarajevo, they would come to Belgrade for specialised training in Belgrade, for a year.
